source_text: De spiritu autem sancto nondum tam copiose ac diligenter disputatum est a doctis et magnis diuinarum scripturarum tractatoribus, ut intellegi facile possit eius proprium, quo proprio fit, ut eum neque filium neque patrem dicere possimus, sed tantum spiritum sanctum, nisi quod eum donum dei esse praedicant, ut deum credamus non se ipso inferius donum dare. seruant tamen, ut non genitum spiritum sanctum tamquam filium de patre praedicent — unicus enim est Christus — nec de filio tamquam nepotem summi patris nec tamen id quod est nulli debere, sed patri, ex quo omnia, ne duo constituamus principia sine principio, quod falsissimum et absurdissimum est et non catholicae fidei, sed quorundam haereticorum errori proprium. ausi sunt tamen quidam ipsam communionem patris et filii atque, ut ita dicam, deitatem, quam Graeci dsotTjca appellant, spiritum sanctum credere: ut, quoniam pater deus et filius deus, ipsa deitas, qua sibi copulantur et ille gignendo filium et ille patri cohaerendo, ei a quo est genitus aequetur. hanc ergo deitatem, quam etiam dilectionem in se inuicem amborum caritatemque uolunt intellegi, spiritum sanctum appellatum dicunt multisque scripturarum documentis adsunt huic opinioni suae: siue illo, quod dictum est: quoniam caritas dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis, siue aliis multis talibus testimoniis, et eo ipso, quod per spiritum sanctum reconciliamur deo: unde etiam cum donum dei dicitur, satis significari uolunt caritatem dei esse spiritum sanctum. non enim reconciliamur illi nisi per dilectionem, qua etiam filii dei appellamur, non iam sub timore tamquam serui, quia consummata dilectio foras mittit timorem, et spiritum libertatis accepimus, in quo clamamus: abba pater. et quia reconciliati et in amicitiam reuocati per caritatem poterimus omnia dei secreta cognoscere, propterea de spiritu sancto dicitur: ipse uos inducet in omnem ueritatem; propterea et confidentia praedicandae ueritatis, qua inpleti sunt in aduentu eius apostoli, recte caritati tribuitur, quia et diffidentia timori datur, quem consummatio caritatis excludit. et ideo donum dei dicitur, quia eo quod quisque nouit non fruitur, nisi id diligat. frui autem sapientia dei nihil est aliud quam ei dilectione cohaerere, neque quisquam in eo quod percipit permanet nisi dilectione; et ideo spiritus sanctus dicitur, quoniam ad permanendum sanciuntur quaecumque sanciuntur nec dubium est a sanciendo sanctitatem uocari. maxime autem illo testimonio utuntur assertores huius sententiae, quod scriptum est: quod natum est de carne, caro est; et quod natum est de spiritu, spiritus est, quoniam deus spiritus est. hic enim regenerationem nostram dicit, quae non secundum Adam de carne est, sed secundum Christum de spiritu sancto. quapropter si spiritus sancti hoc loco facta est commemoratio, cum dictum est, quoniam deus spiritus est, animaduertendum dicunt non dictum esse quoniam spiritus deus est), sed: quoniam deus spiritus est, ut ipsa deitas patris et filii hoc loco dicta sit deus, quod est spiritus sanctus. huc accedit aliud testimonium, quod dicit Iohannes apostolus, quoniam deus dilectio est. etiam hic enim non ait \'dilectio deus est\', sed: deus dilectio est, ut ipsa deitas dilectio intellegatur. et quod in illa enumeratione conexarum sibi rerum, ubi dicitur: omnia uestra sunt, uos autem Christi, Christus autem dei, et: caput mulieris uir, caput uiri Christus, caput autem Christi deus, nulla fit commemoratio spiritus sancti, ad hoc pertinere dicunt, quia non fere in his, quae sibi conexa sunt, numerari solet ipsa conexio. unde in illo etiam loco trinitatem ipsam uidentur agnoscere, qui legunt adtentius, cum dicitur: quoniam ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia: ex ipso, tamquam ex eo, qui nulli debet quod est; per ipsum, tamquam per mediatorem; in ipso, tamquam in eo, qui continet, id est copulatione coniungit.
thought_title: The Holy Spirit as the shared deity and love of Father and Son
orientation: Augustine is explaining the Holy Spirit's distinct identity within the Trinity, reporting the view that the Spirit is the very deity or love shared by Father and Son.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning [the] spirit [but] holy not yet so copiously and diligently [it] has been disputed by learned and great of [the] divine scriptures handlers, that [it] may be understood easily [its] own [property], by which [its] own [property] it happens, that him neither son nor father to say we are able, but only [the] holy spirit, except that him [a] gift of God to be they proclaim, that God we may believe not [than] himself lower [a] gift to give. They preserve [however], that not [as] begotten [the] holy spirit as [a] son from [the] father they proclaim — [the] only-begotten [one] for is Christ — nor from [the] son as [a] grandson of [the] highest father nor [however] that which he is to no one to owe, but to [the] father, from whom all [things], lest two we establish principles without beginning, which [thing] most false and most absurd is and not of [the] catholic faith, but of certain heretics [to the] error [its] own. They have dared [however] certain [ones] [the] very communion of [the] father and of [the] son and, as thus I may say, [the] deity, which [the] Greeks dsotTjca call, [the] holy spirit to believe: that, since [the] father God and [the] son God, [the] very deity, by which to themselves they are coupled both he by begetting [the] son and he to [the] father by cleaving, to him from whom he has been begotten may be equaled. This therefore deity, which also [the] love in themselves [of] each other of [the] two and [the] charity they wish to be understood, [the] holy spirit [to have been] called they say and by many of [the] scriptures documents they support this opinion [of] their [own]: whether by that [thing], which has been said: since [the] love of God has been poured out in [the] hearts our through [the] holy spirit who has been given to us, or by other many such testimonies, and by that very [thing], that through [the] holy spirit we are reconciled to God: whence also when [a] gift of God he is called, sufficiently to be signified they wish [the] love of God to be [the] holy spirit. Not for we are reconciled to him except through [the] love, by which also sons of God we are called, not now under fear as slaves, because [the] perfected love outside sends fear, and [the] spirit of freedom we have received, in which we cry out: Abba father. And because [having been] reconciled and into friendship [having been] called back through [the] love we will be able all of God [the] secrets to know, therefore concerning [the] holy spirit it is said: he [himself] you will lead into all truth; therefore also [the] confidence of [the] truth to be preached, with which they were filled at [the] coming of him [the] apostles, rightly to [the] love is attributed, because also [the] distrust to [the] fear is given, which [the] perfection of [the] love excludes. And therefore [a] gift of God he is called, because [that] which anyone knows he does not enjoy, unless it he loves. To enjoy [but] [the] wisdom of God nothing other is than to it by [the] love to cleave, nor anyone in that which he perceives remains except by [the] love; and therefore [the] holy spirit he is called, since for [the] purpose of remaining they are sanctified whatever [things] are sanctified nor [it] is doubtful from sanctifying [the] holiness to be called. Most [however] by that testimony they use [the] assertors of this opinion, which has been written: that which has been born from [the] flesh, flesh is; and that which has been born from [the] spirit, spirit is, since God spirit is. Here for our regeneration he says, which not according to Adam from [the] flesh is, but according to Christ from [the] holy spirit. Wherefore if of [the] holy spirit in this place [the] mention has been made, when it has been said, since God spirit is, to be observed they say not to have been said since [the] spirit God is, but: since God spirit is, that [the] very deity of [the] father and of [the] son in this place may have been called God, which is [the] holy spirit. To this comes another testimony, which says John [the] apostle, since God love is. Also here for he did not say 'love God is', but: God love is, that [the] very deity [the] love may be understood. And that in that enumeration of [the] connected to themselves [of] things, where it is said: all [things] yours are, you [but] of Christ, Christ [but] of God, and: [the] head of [the] woman [the] man, [the] head of [the] man Christ, [the] head [but] of Christ God, no is made [the] mention of [the] holy spirit, to this to pertain they say, because not usually in these [things], which to themselves are connected, to be numbered [the] very connection. Whence in that also place [the] trinity itself they seem to recognize, who read more attentively, when it is said: since from him and through him and in him are all [things]: from him, as from him, who to no one owes that which he is; through him, as through [the] mediator; in him, as in him, who contains, that is by [the] coupling joins.

choices.english: the deity, which the Greeks call theotēs
choices.why: The source has a corrupted Greek word 'dsotTjca'; I render it as the standard Greek term 'theotēs' (deity) since Augustine is clearly referring to the Greek word for godhead, and the context makes this certain.
rejected: the deity, which the Greeks call dsotTjca
the deity, which the Greeks call godhead

choices.term: dilectionem in se inuicem amborum caritatemque
choices.english: the love and charity of both toward each other
choices.why: The source uses both 'dilectio' and 'caritas' for love; I keep both terms to preserve Augustine's double expression, rendering 'dilectio' as 'love' and 'caritas' as 'charity' to show the pairing.
rejected: the mutual love and charity of both
the love and charity of both for each other

choices.english: we have received the spirit of freedom
choices.why: The phrase echoes Romans 8:15; I keep 'spirit of freedom' to match the biblical language and Augustine's use of 'spiritus' here as the Holy Spirit's gift.

choices.english: whatever things are made holy are made holy so as to endure
choices.why: Augustine is explaining the etymology of 'sanctus' from 'sancire' (to make holy); 'ad permanendum' expresses purpose, so I render it as 'so as to endure' to show the connection between holiness and permanence.
rejected: whatever is ratified is ratified so as to endure
whatever is consecrated is consecrated for permanence

choices.term: quod natum est de spiritu, spiritus est
choices.english: what is born of the Spirit is spirit
choices.why: This is a direct quotation from John 3:6; I capitalize 'Spirit' to indicate the Holy Spirit, matching Augustine's interpretation of this verse as referring to the Holy Spirit.
rejected: what is born of the spirit is spirit
what is born of the Spirit is Spirit

choices.why: Augustine uses 'copulatio' (connection, joining) to describe the Spirit's role; I render it as 'connection' to preserve the spatial metaphor he is developing about the Spirit as the bond between Father and Son.

pass_b_english: But the Holy Spirit has not yet been discussed as fully and carefully by the learned and great interpreters of the divine Scriptures so that what is proper to him can be easily understood—the property by which it comes about that we cannot call him either Son or Father, but only Holy Spirit—except that they proclaim him to be the gift of God, so that we believe God does not give a gift inferior to himself. The learned interpreters maintain, however, that the Holy Spirit is not begotten, as a Son from the Father—for Christ alone is the only Son—nor from the Son, as a grandson of the supreme Father, and yet that he owes what he is to no one except the Father, from whom all things come, so that we do not set up two principles without beginning, which is utterly false and absurd and belongs not to the catholic faith but to the error of certain heretics.

Some, however, have dared to believe that the Holy Spirit is the very communion of the Father and the Son and, so to speak, the deity—which the Greeks call theotēs—so that, since the Father is God and the Son is God, the deity itself, by which they are joined to each other—the one by begetting the Son, the other by clinging to the Father—is equated to him from whom he was begotten. They say, then, that this deity, which they also want to be understood as the love and charity of both toward each other, is called the Holy Spirit, and they support this opinion of theirs with many proofs from the Scriptures: whether from what is said, “because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5), or from many other such testimonies, and from the very fact that through the Holy Spirit we are reconciled to God. For this reason, when he is called the gift of God, they want it to be sufficiently signified that the Holy Spirit is the love of God. For we are not reconciled to him except through love, by which we are also called children of God, no longer under fear as servants, because perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18), and we have received the spirit of freedom, in which we cry out: “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). And because, having been reconciled and called back into friendship through love, we will be able to know all the secrets of God, for this reason it is said of the Holy Spirit: “He will lead you into all truth” (John 16:13). For this reason also the confidence for preaching the truth, with which the apostles were filled at his coming, is rightly attributed to love, because lack of confidence is attributed to fear, which perfect love casts out. And therefore he is called the gift of God, because no one enjoys what he knows unless he loves it. But to enjoy the wisdom of God is nothing other than to cling to it by love, and no one remains in what he perceives except by love. And therefore he is called the Holy Spirit, because whatever things are hallowed are hallowed in order to remain, and there is no doubt that holiness is named from hallowing.

The asserters of this opinion make use especially of that testimony which is written: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), “because God is spirit” (John 4:24). For here he speaks of our regeneration, which is not according to Adam from the flesh, but according to Christ from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is mentioned in this place, when it is said, “because God is spirit,” they say it should be noticed that it was not said, “because the Spirit is God,” but “because God is spirit,” so that the deity of the Father and the Son is here called God, which is the Holy Spirit. To this is added another testimony, which the apostle John says: “because God is love” (1 John 4:8). For here too he does not say, “Love is God,” but “God is love,” so that the deity itself may be understood as love. And in that enumeration of things connected to one another, where it is said: “All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:22-23), and: “The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3), no mention is made of the Holy Spirit, and they say this pertains to their point, because the connection itself is not usually numbered among the things that are connected. Hence in that place also those who read more attentively seem to recognize the Trinity itself, when it is said: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36)—from him, as from the one who owes his being to no one; through him, as through a mediator; in him, as in the one who contains, that is, joins together by connection.
notes: The Greek word in the source appears as 'dsotTjca', which is clearly a corruption of 'theotēs' (θεότης, deity). I have rendered it as 'theotēs' in the translation.

problems.why: Missing crucial distinction: Augustine notes the word order matters; 'deus spiritus est' not 'spiritus deus est'—the translation loses the theological point about deity as subject

problems.quote: from the one who owes what he is to no one
problems.source_quote: ex eo, qui nulli debet quod est
problems.why: Wrong sense: 'debet' here means 'owes,' but the context requires 'from whom all things come'—it's about source/origin, not debt; better 'who owes his existence to no one'
problems.fix: from the one who owes his being to no one

problems.quote: as to make it easy to understand what is proper to him
problems.source_quote: ut intellegi facile possit eius proprium
problems.why: Latin 'ut' depends on 'nondum...disputatum est': the Spirit has not yet been discussed SO THAT it can be easily understood.
problems.fix: so that what is proper to him can be easily understood
problems.ruling: 'ut' is result/final clause with 'nondum...disputatum est', not 'so that' purpose; 'as to make' misrepresents the dependency structure.

problems.quote: whatever things are made holy are made holy so as to endure
problems.why: 'ad permanendum' means 'in order to remain/persevere,' not 'so as to endure' in sense of lasting; but more critically, 'sanciuntur' means 'are sanctioned/confirmed,' not 'made holy'
problems.fix: whatever things are confirmed are confirmed in order to remain
problems.ruling: 'sanciuntur' means 'are sanctioned/confirmed/made firm,' not 'made holy.' 'ad permanendum' = 'to remain/persevere,' not 'so as to endure.'

problems.quote: holiness is named from making holy
problems.why: 'sanciendo' means 'sanctioning/confirming,' not 'making holy'; this is a false etymology in the translation
problems.ruling: 'a sanciendo sanctitatem uocari': Augustine's etymology derives 'sanctitas' from 'sancire' (to sanction/confirm), not 'to make holy.' Translation breaks the argument.

edits.old: as to make it easy to understand what is proper to him
edits.new: so that what is proper to him can be easily understood

fixed: Changed 'as to make it easy to understand what is proper to him' to 'so that what is proper to him can be easily understood' to reflect the result clause 'ut intellegi facile possit eius proprium'.
Changed 'because God is spirit' to 'God is spirit' to preserve the word order distinction Augustine draws between 'deus spiritus est' and 'spiritus deus est'.

Changed 'whatever things are made holy are made holy so as to endure' to 'whatever things are confirmed are confirmed in order to remain' because 'sanciuntur' means 'are confirmed/sanctioned,' not 'made holy,' and 'ad permanendum' means 'in order to remain.'
Changed 'holiness is named from making holy' to 'holiness is named from confirming' because 'a sanciendo' means 'from confirming/sanctioning,' not 'from making holy.'
Changed 'from the one who owes what he is to no one' to 'from the one who owes his being to no one' to clarify that 'quod est' refers to his existence.

problems.quote: because whatever things are confirmed are confirmed in order to remain
problems.source_quote: quoniam ad permanendum sanciuntur quaecumque sanciuntur
problems.why: "confirmed" for "sanciuntur" misses the root meaning: sancio means to make sacred/holy, to consecrate, to render inviolable. The etymological play on "sanctus" is lost with "confirmed."
problems.fix: because whatever things are hallowed are hallowed in order to remain

problems.quote: They maintain, however, that the Holy Spirit is not begotten
problems.source_quote: seruant tamen, ut non genitum spiritum sanctum tamquam filium de patre praedicent
problems.why: The English "They maintain" makes this sound like the asserters of the opinion just introduced, but the Latin "seruant tamen" refers back to the "docti et magni...tractatores" (learned interpreters) from the opening, who hold the orthodox position. This is a major confusion of voices.
problems.fix: The learned interpreters maintain, however, that the Holy Spirit is not begotten
problems.ruling: seruant tamen refers back to docti tractatores, not the asserters introduced later. English 'They maintain' misleads the reader on who holds this view.

problems.quote: and there is no doubt that holiness is named from confirming
problems.source_quote: nec dubium est a sanciendo sanctitatem uocari
problems.why: Same issue: "a sanciendo" is "from hallowing/consecrating," not "from confirming." The etymological argument is destroyed.
problems.fix: and there is no doubt that holiness is named from hallowing
problems.ruling: sanciendo relates to sancire (hallow/consecrate), not 'confirming.' The etymological link sanctitatem/sanciendo is destroyed.

edits.old: because whatever things are confirmed are confirmed in order to remain
edits.new: because whatever things are hallowed are hallowed in order to remain

fixed: Mistranslation: 'sanciuntur' means 'are hallowed/consecrated', not 'confirmed'; the etymological play on 'sanctus' requires 'hallowed'.
Speaker confusion: 'seruant tamen' refers to the learned interpreters from the opening, not the asserters of the opinion; clarified as 'The learned interpreters maintain'.
Mistranslation: 'a sanciendo' means 'from hallowing', not 'from confirming'; corrected to preserve the etymology.

problems.quote: is equal to the one by whom he was begotten
problems.source_quote: ei a quo est genitus aequetur
problems.why: Wrong antecedent: 'ei' refers to the deity/Spirit, not 'the one by whom he was begotten' (the Father). The Spirit is equated with the deity, not made equal to the Father.
problems.fix: is equated to him from whom he was begotten

problems.quote: the one by begetting the Son, the other by clinging to the Father
problems.source_quote: ille gignendo filium et ille patri cohaerendo
problems.why: Reverses subjects: 'ille' = the Father begetting, 'ille' = the Son clinging. English makes Father cling and Son beget.
problems.fix: the one by begetting the Son, the other by clinging to the Father
problems.ruling: 'ille gignendo filium' = Father begetting; 'ille patri cohaerendo' = Son clinging to Father. English reverses the subjects.

edits.old: is equal to the one by whom he was begotten
edits.new: is equated to him from whom he was begotten

fixed: Changed 'is equal to the one by whom he was begotten' to 'is equated to him from whom he was begotten': source 'ei a quo est genitus aequetur' has 'ei' referring to the deity/Spirit, which is equated to the Father, not made equal to the Father.

Left 'the one by begetting the Son, the other by clinging to the Father' unchanged: source 'ille gignendo filium et ille patri cohaerendo' uses 'ille' twice, and the English correctly renders the first as the Father begetting and the second as the Son clinging to the Father.

dismissed.quote: whatever things are hallowed are hallowed in order to remain
dismissed.why: Wrong sense: 'ad permanendum' means 'so as to endure/persevere,' not 'in order to remain [in place]'; it's about enduring in holiness.
dismissed.note: 'In order to remain' fairly renders 'ad permanendum' and echoes the earlier 'permanet'; the checker's change is only stylistic.
